title: What someone said
verifiedBy: LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: Reporting moves the verb back one step, exactly as English does: dice que viene becomes dijo que venía, and dice que vendrá becomes dijo que vendría. The present goes to the IMPERFECT — L2-M10's tense doing a second job — and the future goes to the conditional, which is M4's. Nothing new is opened for either, and an English speaker's instinct is already right.

A yes-or-no question is reported with si and never with que: me preguntó si tenía tiempo. English says "asked me that" nowhere and "asked me if" everywhere, and yet que is what a learner reaches for, because que is the word every other reported clause takes. A wh-question keeps its own word and its accent: me preguntó dónde estaba el baño.

The object pronouns la, los and las are spelled exactly like L1-M1's articles la, los and las, and they are different words. Nothing in the spelling separates them — only the position does: in front of a verb it is an object, in front of a noun it is an article. Las llaves no están aquí, las tengo en casa: both las in one breath, two different words.

The object goes BEFORE a conjugated verb — la vi, los conozco — and may ride on the end of an infinitive: voy a verla. One choice, two spellings, and both are ordinary. Two objects in one sentence (se lo dije) is a later level's, and this module never shows one.

sentences.display: Dice que viene hoy. Dijo que venía el sábado.
sentences.cue: He says he's coming today. He said he was coming on Saturday.
sentences.literal: Says that comes today. Said that was-coming the Saturday.

words.note: The present of decir, beside L2-M10's dijo and M4's diré. The stem vowel breaks to i under the stress, which is why it is not dece.
The present of venir, whose future M4 taught as vendré. The e breaks to ie under the stress: viene, but venir and venía.
The imperfect of venir — L2-M10's tense doing the reporting job. The stress moves off the stem, so the ie heals back to a plain e.

sentences.trap: Nothing here is a Spanish rule an English speaker has to learn; it is the same step back English takes in "he said he was coming". The work is in the cells, not in the grammar.
sentences.sound: DI-se and BIE-ne, both stressed at the front. be-NI-a is three syllables and the accent breaks the i from the a.

variations.cue: He said he was coming today.
variations.changed: the day the coming was promised for

variations.cue: He says he's coming on Sunday.
variations.changed: the unreported half given a new day

mistake.why: Once the saying is in the past the clause moves back with it: dijo que venía. viene there is the sentence still being said, not reported.

sentences.usage: Passing on a message. Both halves in one item so the step back is visible rather than described.
sentences.mnemonic: The saying moves back and the clause follows.

sentences.display: Dice que vendrá mañana. Dijo que vendría hoy.
sentences.cue: He says he'll come tomorrow. He said he'd come today.
sentences.literal: Says that will-come tomorrow. Said that would-come today.

words.note: M4's vendré with the ending for he or she: vendré, vendrá. The shortened stem vendr- is the same in every cell of the tense.
The conditional of venir, off the same vendr- stem: vendrá, vendría. It is what a reported future becomes, and nothing else changes.

sentences.trap: The future does not stay a future when it is reported. English does the same thing — "he'll come" becomes "he'd come" — so the shape is new and the move is not.
sentences.sound: ben-DRA and ben-DRI-a, the second a syllable longer with the stress on the i.

variations.cue: He said he'd come on Sunday.
variations.changed: the day he promised

variations.cue: He says he'll come on Saturday.
variations.changed: the promise still in the present

mistake.why: A reported future takes the conditional: dijo que vendría hoy. vendrá keeps the promise in the speaker's own mouth rather than in the one being quoted.

sentences.usage: The version of S01 for a promise rather than a plan. Both are ordinary and the choice is only about how far off the coming was.

sentences.cue: He asked me if I had time.

words.note: Asking a question is preguntar; asking FOR a thing is pedir, a different verb. Spanish never uses one for the other, where English uses "ask" for both.
The imperfect of tener, which is what a reported tengo becomes. L2-M10's era and estaba are built the same way, and one cell covers yo and él/ella.

sentences.trap: This si is M4's word doing a second job: not a condition here, but "whether". The one thing it can never be replaced by is que.
sentences.sound: pre-gun-TO, stressed on the last syllable, which is what the accent marks. te-NI-a in three syllables.

variations.cue: He asked me if I was coming today.
variations.changed: what was being asked about

variations.cue: He asked him if he had time.
variations.changed: who was asked, with L2-M7's le

mistake.why: A yes-or-no question is reported with si: me preguntó si tenía tiempo. que is what every other reported clause takes, and that is exactly why it lands here.

sentences.usage: Reporting a question you were asked, which is most of what gets reported at work.
sentences.mnemonic: A question reports with si, not que.

sentences.display: Me preguntó dónde estaba el baño. No lo sabía.
sentences.cue: He asked me where the toilet was. I didn't know.
sentences.literal: To-me asked where was the bathroom. Not it I-knew.

words.note: The imperfect of saber, beside L3-M2's sé. Knowing is a state, so the reported past of it is almost always this tense rather than the preterite.

sentences.trap: The wh-word keeps its accent inside the report. dónde is still a question word even with no question mark anywhere in the sentence.
sentences.sound: sa-BI-a, three syllables. The accent on dónde marks it as the question word and changes nothing about how it is said.

variations.display: Me preguntó dónde estaba la estación.
variations.cue: He asked me where the station was.
variations.changed: what was being looked for

variations.cue: He asked me what I wanted.
variations.changed: a different wh-word, accent and all

mistake.display: Me preguntó donde estaba el baño.
mistake.why: The accent belongs to the question word and survives the reporting: me preguntó dónde estaba. Bare donde is the joining word in la casa donde vivo.

sentences.usage: Telling somebody about an exchange you could not help with. The second sentence is the clitic lo doing quiet work.
sentences.mnemonic: A reported question keeps its accent.

sentences.display: La vi ayer en el parque.
sentences.cue: I saw her yesterday in the park.
sentences.literal: Her I-saw yesterday in the park.

words.cue: I saw her · I saw it
words.note: The la in front of a verb is "her", not L1-M1's "the". Same spelling, different word, and only the position says which: la vi against la casa.

sentences.trap: English puts the object after the verb and Spanish puts it in front, which means the sentence opens on a word that looks like an article. La vi is never "the saw".
sentences.sound: la BI, two quick syllables with the stress on the second. The v is a soft b made with both lips.

variations.display: Las vi ayer en la tienda.
variations.cue: I saw them yesterday in the shop.
variations.changed: one woman to several, and the place

variations.cue: I saw her this morning.
variations.changed: when the seeing happened

mistake.display: Vi la ayer en el parque.
mistake.why: The object stands in front of a conjugated verb: la vi ayer. English's order is what puts it behind, and behind the verb it reads as an unfinished article.

sentences.usage: Ordinary gossip. The object is in front because that is where Spanish keeps it, and nothing about the word order is emphatic.
sentences.mnemonic: In front of a verb, la is her.

sentences.display: Los conozco muy bien. Son amigos de mi hermana.
sentences.cue: I know them very well. They're friends of my sister's.
sentences.literal: Them I-know very well. Are friends of my sister.

words.note: los in front of a verb is "them", not L1-M1's "the". L3-M2's conozco is untouched — it is the object that arrived, not a new verb.

sentences.trap: los conozco and los amigos start with the same three letters and share nothing else. The verb behind it is what makes the first one a pronoun.
sentences.sound: los ko-NOS-ko, said as one run. The s at the end of los links straight into the k with no pause.

variations.cue: I know them from work.
variations.changed: where you know them from

variations.cue: I don't know them very well.
variations.changed: the negative, with no in front of the pair

mistake.why: The object goes in front: los conozco muy bien. Behind the verb, los is left waiting for a noun that never comes.

sentences.usage: Placing people for somebody who has just met them. The second sentence is what makes the first one polite rather than curt.
sentences.mnemonic: A verb behind it makes it them.

sentences.display: Las llaves no están aquí. Las tengo en casa.
sentences.cue: The keys aren't here. I've got them at home.
sentences.literal: The keys not are here. Them I-have in house.

words.note: The second las of this item is "them" and the first is "the". Nothing but the word after it tells them apart: las llaves, las tengo.

sentences.trap: Both words are in one item on purpose. The article leans on a noun and the pronoun leans on a verb, and that is the whole of the difference a reader gets.
sentences.sound: las TEN-go, with the s running into the t. The pair is said as one word with no gap.

variations.cue: I've got them here.
variations.changed: where they are

variations.cue: I don't have them.
variations.changed: the negative, and the object still in front

mistake.why: The object stands in front of the verb: las tengo en casa. Behind it, las reads as an article waiting for its noun.

sentences.usage: The everyday answer to "where are the keys". Naming the keys twice would sound like an explanation rather than an answer.
sentences.mnemonic: las before a noun is the; before a verb is them.

sentences.display: Lo dije ayer. Le dije que no sabía nada.
sentences.cue: I said it yesterday. I told him I didn't know anything.
sentences.literal: It I-said yesterday. To-him I-said that not I-knew nothing.

words.note: lo is the thing said and le is the person told: lo dije, le dije. L2-M5's lo and L2-M7's le are those two rows, and the verb is the same.

sentences.trap: One letter separates lo dije from le dije, and they answer different questions. What was said takes lo; who was told takes le.
sentences.sound: lo DI-he, with the j of dije a breathy h. The two clipped words run together.

variations.cue: I told him I was coming today.
variations.changed: what was reported to him

variations.cue: I said it this morning.
variations.changed: when it was said

mistake.display: Le dije ayer, no lo dije a él.
mistake.why: lo is what was said and le is who heard it, so the two never stand in for each other: lo dije ayer, le dije que no sabía nada.

sentences.usage: Defending yourself in a conversation about who knew what. Both pronouns are needed, and neither is optional.
sentences.mnemonic: lo is what; le is who.

sentences.display: Voy a verla mañana. La vi ayer también.
sentences.cue: I'm going to see her tomorrow. I saw her yesterday too.
sentences.literal: I-go to to-see-her tomorrow. Her I-saw yesterday also.

words.note: L1-M6's ver with the object stuck on its end — one word on the page and two pieces in the grammar. L3-M1's ducharme is built exactly the same way.

sentences.trap: Two positions, one meaning. The object rides the infinitive and stands in front of a conjugated verb, and neither order is more correct than the other.
sentences.sound: ber-LA, stressed on the end because the object added a syllable and the stress came with it.

variations.cue: I'm going to see her on Saturday.
variations.changed: the day

variations.cue: I'm not going to see her today.
variations.changed: the plan dropped, with the object still on the infinitive

mistake.why: On an infinitive the object goes on the end and is written as one word: voy a verla. Standing it in front only works when the verb is conjugated.

sentences.usage: A plan and the reason it is not urgent. The two positions in one item are what make the choice visible.

sentences.display: Me preguntó si quería ir. Le dije que sí.
sentences.cue: He asked me if I wanted to go. I told him yes.
sentences.literal: To-me asked if I-wanted to-go. To-him I-said that yes.

words.note: The imperfect of querer, which is what a reported quiero becomes. It is also the softest way to ask for something, and that use is a later module's.

sentences.trap: si and sí are both in this item, four words apart. The first is "whether" and the second is "yes", and the accent is the only thing separating them.
sentences.sound: ke-RI-a, three syllables with the stress on the i. The si and the sí are said identically; only the writing differs.

variations.cue: He asked me if I wanted coffee.
variations.changed: what was offered

variations.display: Le dije que no podré ir.
variations.cue: I told him I won't be able to go.
variations.changed: the answer, with M4's future kept as it was said

mistake.why: The whether-si carries no accent: me preguntó si quería ir. Written with one, it is the yes that belongs at the end of the item instead.

sentences.usage: The whole module in two lines: a reported question, a backshifted verb, and an answer given with le. Nothing here is new except the tense on querer.
sentences.mnemonic: si asks it; sí answers it.
